Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 101, verses 1–3:

Page 67
(Surat al-Qari'ah)
Eleven verses, Meccan

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿The Striking Calamity﴾ ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ Know that when Allah, glorified and exalted, concluded the preceding surah with His saying: ﴿Indeed, their Lord is Well-Acquainted with them that Day﴾, it is as if it were said: "And what is that Day?" So it was said: "It is the Striking Calamity."

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿The Striking Calamity﴾ ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ Know that in this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-qar' (striking) is striking with force and pressure. Then the great event among the events of time was named "qari'ah" (striking calamity). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve for what they have done﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. From it comes the saying: "The slave is struck (yuqra') with the stick," and from it comes al-miqra'ah (the whip/striking rod), and qawari' al-Qur'an (the striking verses of the Qur'an), and qara'a al-bab (he knocked on the door). And taqara'u means they struck one another with swords. They agreed that al-Qari'ah is one of the names of the Resurrection, and they differed regarding the reason (lima) for this naming, in several ways:

The first: the reason for that is the Blast by which all creatures die, because in the first Blast minds depart, as Allah said: ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall unconscious﴾ [al-Zumar: 68]. In the second, all creatures die except Israfil; then Allah causes him to die and then revives him, and he blows the third, and they stand up. It is narrated that the Trumpet has a hole for each of the dead, a specific hole for each one, so Allah revives every body by that blast reaching it through that specific hole. What confirms this view is His saying: ﴿They await but a single Blast﴾ [Ya-Sin: 49], and ﴿It will be but a single shout﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13].

The second: the upper and lower celestial bodies collide violently when the world is destroyed, and because of that striking the Day of Resurrection was named al-Qari'ah.

The third: al-Qari'ah is that which strikes people with terrors and fright; this occurs in the heavens through splitting and cleaving, in the sun and moon through being folded up, in the stars through being scattered, in the mountains through being crushed and blown away, and in the earth through being flattened and changed. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The fourth: it strikes the enemies of Allah with punishment, disgrace and retribution. This is the view of Muqatil. Some of the verifiers said: this is more preferable than the view of al-Kalbi

Page 68
because of His saying: ﴿and they will be safe from terror that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89].

The second issue: regarding the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of His saying: ﴿al-Qari'ah﴾ ﴿ma al-Qari'ah﴾, there are several views:

The first: it is a warning (tahdhir). Warnings come in both the nominative and accusative forms; you say: "The lion! The lion!" so both raf' and nasb are permissible.

The second: there is an implied element (idmar), meaning: "The Striking Calamity will come upon you," in accordance with what I informed about in His saying: ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 9].

The third: it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and its predicate is: ﴿ma al-Qari'ah﴾. According to the view of Qutrub, the predicate is: ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾. If it is said: when you inform about something with something, you must gain from it additional knowledge, and His saying ﴿And what will make you know﴾ indicates that he is ignorant of it, so how can this be conceived as a predicate? We say: we have gained from this predicate additional knowledge, because we used to think it was a striking calamity like the other calamities, and by this mystification we learned that it is a calamity that surpasses all calamities in terror and severity.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ has several views:

The first: its meaning is that you have no knowledge of its reality, because in its severity it is such that no one's imagination or understanding can reach it, and however you estimate it, it is greater than your estimation. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: the calamities of this world, in comparison with that calamity, are as if they were not calamities, and the fire of this world, in comparison with the fire of the Hereafter, is as if it were not fire. For this reason He said at the end of the surah: ﴿A blazing Fire﴾, drawing attention to the fact that the fire of this world, in comparison with that, is not blazing, and the end of the surah thus corresponds to its beginning in this respect. If it is said: here He said ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ and at the end of the surah He said: ﴿Then his mother will be an abyss﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ and He did not say "And what will make you know what the Abyss is?" So what is the difference? We say: the difference is that its being a striking calamity is a matter that is perceived, whereas its being an abyss is not like that; so the difference between the two places is evident.

The second: no one has a path to knowing that detail except through Allah's informing and explaining it, because it is an inquiry into the occurrence of events, not into the obligation of obligatory matters, so there is no proof for knowing it except through revelation (sam').

The fourth issue: a parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿The Inevitable Reality﴾ ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 1–3]. Then the verifiers said: His saying ﴿al-Qari'ah﴾ ﴿ma al-Qari'ah﴾ is stronger than His saying ﴿al-Haqqah﴾ ﴿ma al-Haqqah﴾, because what is revealed later must be more eloquent, since its purpose is to increase alertness, and this increase is only achieved if it is stronger. As for considering the meaning, al-Haqqah is more severe because it refers to the meaning of justice, while al-Qari'ah is more severe in that it assaults hearts with a terrifying matter.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ ﴿and the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The adverbial of time (ẓarf) is in the accusative because it is governed by an implied verb, which is indicated by al-Qari'ah (the Striking Calamity). That is, "It strikes on the Day when mankind will be such-and-such."

Know that He, exalted is He, described that Day with two matters:

The first: the state of mankind in it: ﴿like scattered moths﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-farash is the creature that hurls itself into the fire, and it is called farash because of its spreading out and dispersing. Then He, exalted is He, compared the creation at the time of resurrection here to scattered moths, and in another verse to scattered locusts. As for the aspect of comparison with moths, it is because when moths rise up they do not head in one direction; rather, each of them goes off in a direction other than the direction of the others. This indicates that when they are resurrected they will be terrified and will disagree about their aims, going in various directions that are not known. Al-mabthuth means "scattered," as one says: "He scattered it (baththahu) when he separated it." As for the aspect of comparison with locusts, it is in multitude. Al-Farra' said: "Like the swarming locusts, some of which climb upon others." In sum, God, glory be to Him, compared people at the time of resurrection to scattered locusts and scattered moths, because when they are resurrected, some of them surge over others like locusts and moths. What we have mentioned is confirmed by His saying: ﴿so you will come in throngs﴾ [al-Naba' 78:18], His saying: ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin 83:6], and His saying concerning the story of Gog and Magog: ﴿And We will leave some of them that Day surging over others﴾ [al-Kahf 18:99].

If it is said: Locusts are large in comparison with moths, so how can He compare one thing to both the small and the large at once? We say: He compared the one thing to the small and the large, but in two respects. As for the comparison to moths, it is by each one going off in a direction other than the direction of the others. As for the comparison to locusts, it is by multitude and succession. It may also be said that they will at first be large like locusts, and then become small like moths because of their being scorched by the heat of the sun.

They also mentioned several other aspects of the comparison with moths:

One of them: what has been narrated, that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "People are of two kinds: a scholar and a learner, and the rest of people are worthless rabble (hamaj ra'a')." So God will make them such on the Last Day: ﴿a fitting recompense﴾ [al-Naba' 78:26].

Another: He, exalted is He, introduced the particle of comparison, saying ﴿like moths﴾, because on that Day they will be more abased than moths, for moths are not punished, whereas these will be punished. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿They are like cattle; nay, they are even more astray﴾ [al-A'raf 7:179].

The second attribute of that Day is His saying: ﴿and the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾. Al-'ihn is wool of various colors, and its verification has already passed under His saying: ﴿and the mountains will be like 'ihn﴾. Al-naf is unteasing the wool until some of it separates from other parts of it. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "like fluffed-up wool (al-suf al-manfush)."

Know that God, exalted is He, informed that the mountains are of various colors, as He said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying hues, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir 35:27]. Then He, glory be to Him, separates their parts and removes the cohesion and composition from them, so that this becomes similar to wool dyed in various colors when it is made fluffed-up. Here there are several issues:

First issue: He only joined the state of mankind with the state of the mountains, as if He, exalted is He, were alerting that the effect of that striking calamity on the mountains is that they become like fluffed-up wool. So how will the human being be when he hears it? Then woe, and again woe, to the son of Adam if the mercy of his Lord does not overtake him. It may also be that what is meant is that the mountains of the Fire will become like fluffed-up wool because of the intensity of their redness.

Second issue: God, exalted is He, has described the changing of conditions upon the mountains in several ways:

First: that they become pieces, as He said: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded to powder﴾ [al-Fajr 89:21].

Second: that they become a heap of sand that flows, as He said: ﴿You see the mountains and think them solid, yet they pass by like clouds﴾ [al-Naml 27:88]. Then they become like fluffed-up wool, being parts like dust-motes that enter through a window of the house and that no hand can touch. Then, in the fourth stage, He said: they become a mirage, as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and become a mirage﴾ [al-Naba' 78:20].

Third issue: He did not say, "On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths and the mountains like fluffed-up wool," but rather said: ﴿and the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾, because repetition in such a context is more forceful in giving warning.

Know that God, exalted is He, informed that the mountains are of various colors, as He said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying hues, and jet-black﴾ [Fatir 35:27]. Then He, glory be to Him, separates their parts and removes the cohesion and composition from them, so that this becomes similar to wool dyed in various colors when it is made fluffed-up. Here there are several issues:

First issue: He only joined the state of mankind with the state of the mountains, as if He, exalted is He, were alerting that the effect of that striking calamity on the mountains is that they become like fluffed-up wool. So how will the human being be when he hears it? Then woe, and again woe, to the son of Adam if the mercy of his Lord does not overtake him. It may also be that what is meant is that the mountains of the Fire will become like fluffed-up wool because of the intensity of their redness.

Second issue: God, exalted is He, has described the changing of conditions upon the mountains in several ways:

First: that they become pieces, as He said: ﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded to powder﴾ [al-Fajr 89:21].

Second: that they become a heap of sand that flows, as He said: ﴿You see the mountains and think them solid, yet they pass by like clouds﴾ [al-Naml 27:88]. Then they become like fluffed-up wool, being parts like dust-motes that enter through a window of the house and that no hand can touch. Then, in the fourth stage, He said: they become a mirage, as He said: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and become a mirage﴾ [al-Naba' 78:20].

Third issue: He did not say, "On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths and the mountains like fluffed-up wool," but rather said: ﴿and the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾, because repetition in such a context is more forceful in giving warning.

Here is the translation:

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the Day of Resurrection, He divided people into two categories in it, so He said: ﴿As for him whose scales are heavy﴾. Know that regarding the scales (mawazin) there are two opinions:

The first: that it is the plural of mawzun (the weighed), which is the deed that has weight and worth with Allah. This is the view of al-Farra'. He said: An analogous usage is said: "I have a dirham equal in weight (bimizan) to your dirham and its weight (wazn), and my house is equal in measure (bimizan) to your house and its weight (wazn)," meaning: equal to it.

The second: that it is the plural of mizan (balance). Ibn 'Abbas said: The mizan has a tongue and two pans; only deeds are weighed in it. The good deeds of the obedient person are brought in their most beautiful form, and if they outweigh, then Paradise is his. The evil deeds of the disbeliever are brought in their ugliest form, so his weight becomes light and he enters the Fire. al-Hasan said regarding the mizan: it has two pans and is not described further. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: The good and evil deeds themselves cannot properly be weighed, especially since they have already ceased to exist. Rather, what is meant is that the scrolls in which the good and evil deeds are written are weighed, or light is made a sign of good deeds and darkness a sign of evil deeds, or the scroll of good deeds is depicted in a beautiful form and the scroll of evil deeds in an ugly form, so that heaviness and lightness become apparent. The benefit of this is that the state of the doer of good deeds becomes manifest before the great assembly, so he rejoices more, and the state of the doer of evil deeds becomes manifest, which is a disgrace to him before all creation.

As for His saying: ﴿then he will be in a pleasant life﴾, "al-'ishah" is a verbal noun meaning "al-'aysh" (life), like "al-khifah" meaning "al-khawf" (fear). As for "al-radiyah", al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: a life possessed of contentment (ridan), which its owner is pleased with. It is like their saying "labin" and "tamir", meaning "possessor of milk" and "possessor of dates". For this reason the exegetes said: its explanation is "marḍiyyah" (pleasing), in the sense that its owner is pleased with it.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And as for him whose scales are light﴾, meaning: whose good deeds are few, so the evil deeds outweigh the good deeds. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The scales of those whose scales are heavy are heavy only because they followed the truth in this world and it was heavy upon them; and it is right that a balance into which only the truth is placed should be heavy. The scales of those whose scales are light are light only because they followed falsehood in this world and it was light upon them; and it is right that a balance into which falsehood is placed should be light. Muqatil said: It is so because truth is heavy and falsehood is light.

﴿So his mother is an abyss﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ ﴿A blazing fire﴾. As for His saying: ﴿So his mother is an abyss﴾, there are several opinions:

The first: that al-Hawiyah is one of the names of the Fire, as if it were the deep fire into which the people of the Fire plunge (yahwi) a far plunge. The meaning is: his refuge is the Fire. It was said that the refuge is called "umm" (mother) by way of comparison with the mother, to whom a child flees in fear alone.

The second: "his mother's head is in the Fire, an abyss", related by al-Akhfash, al-Kalbi, and Qatadah, who said: because they fall headlong into the Fire on their heads.

The third: when they invoke destruction upon a man they say: "May his mother fall (hawat ummuhu)", because when he falls (hawa), i.e. perishes and is destroyed, his mother has fallen in grief and bereavement. So it is as if it was said: "As for him whose scales are light", then he has perished.
